source.title: Finding Neurons in a Haystack: Case Studies with Sparse Probing
source.authors: Wes Gurnee; Neel Nanda; Matthew Pauly; Katherine Harvey; Dmitrii Troitskii; D. Bertsimas

page_placements.theme: Neuron importance, monosemanticity and splitting change with language-model scale

record.tranche_reason: The study uses sparse probes, corpus activation analyses, and ablations to investigate neuron specialization and polysemanticity in language models, rather than reproducing the original vision-model method.
record.gate_note: The paper directly reports language-model neurons responding to apparently unrelated inputs and discusses how probe design and activation inspection affect interpretation. It does not measure the fraction of all neurons that are polysemantic. Cited findings from other work and the weight-statistic proxy for superposition are not recorded as standalone results here; the aggregate scale sweeps report feature sparsity rather than polysemantic-neuron prevalence.
record.test_reason: In Pythia language models the study finds early-layer MLP neurons that fire on many unrelated n-grams (V2). It treats these as superposition, using sparse combinations, basis-alignment tests and weight statistics (V3). It also shows that neuron interpretation changes with the corpus, top-k examples and scoring metric (V7). This uses a different method (sparse probing plus corpus inspection) on the question the SoLU original addressed.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly right. The authors conclude that early layers represent many features, especially n-grams, in superposition as sparse combinations of massively polysemantic neurons. Weight statistics suggest roughly the first 25% of layers use substantially more superposition. Middle layers have seemingly monosemantic context neurons, though monosemanticity is hard to prove. Representational sparsity rises with scale on average, with varied per-feature dynamics. Sparse probing needs careful follow-up analysis to avoid interpretability illusions.
record.recipe_differences: Uses supervised sparse probing to locate candidate neurons, then examines activations and performs selected ablations; it is not the original vision-model neuron-analysis procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: Interpretation depends on the probe dataset and feature definition, the examples or corpus used to inspect activations, and the use of summary metrics versus raw activation counts. The reported effect of context-neuron ablation also differs with model size.

fits_no_version.finding: Representational sparsity (k-sparse probe F1) rises on average with model size, with feature-specific dynamics such as emergence of dedicated neurons and splitting (Sec 5.3, Figs 4, 7, 18).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sparsity of feature representations in LMs changes with model scale in feature-dependent ways.

fits_no_version.finding: Context-neuron ablation impact falls sharply with model size (8% at 70M vs 0.2% at 6.9B).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Single-neuron importance decreases with model scale.

record.problems: The authors note that probing can be sensitive to dataset misspecification, spurious correlations, feature granularity, and rare features; it offers limited causal insight and can confuse superposition with composition. Monosemanticity is difficult to prove, and the study's models are from one family trained on the same data. The selected-neuron case studies do not quantify the prevalence of polysemantic neurons, and no uncertainty estimates are stated for the reported case-study outcomes.
record.rows_left_out: No rows were left out under the row limit. Aggregate feature-sparsity scaling results and early-layer weight-statistic distributions were not included because they do not directly measure polysemantic-neuron prevalence or the behavior named by the claim versions.

untested.parts: All of it: vision classifiers and InceptionV1.
The share of all MLP neurons that are polysemantic. Only selected neurons are inspected, and layer differences rest on a weight-statistic proxy.
A causal test that capacity pressure produces the observed polysemantic neurons. The 'more features than neurons' premise is argued, not measured.
All of it: initialization, regularization or noise as causes when capacity is sufficient.
All of it. No activation-function, architecture or regularization comparison; model-size sweeps only.
Canonical vision examples (e.g. InceptionV1 car/cat neurons), and whether unrelated mixtures are rare overall.
No systematic sweep over activation ranges or explanation-scoring methods; case studies only.

missing.what: Product of input weight norm and bias per neuron across all layers and models. Early layers (~first 25%) stand out, which the authors take as a superposition fingerprint. This is a proxy, not a polysemanticity count.
Basis-alignment test: neuron basis vs random basis on compound-word classification (top-50 F1, and logistic loss vs k) in layers 1-4 of Pythia 1B.
n-gram polysemanticity of layer 1 neuron 0 in all seven Pythia models.
Middle-layer context neurons (French, Go, Pile subsets) that activate approximately only in their target context, shown as activation distributions in vs out of context. Bears on layer variation.
Athlete-type neurons reinterpreted as general sport neurons from per-token average activations rather than max-activating examples. The hockey neuron appears to be a Canadian neuron.

record.verdict_notes: The authors also argue, without testing it, that attempts to remove superposition such as SoLU probably hide it or are not competitive. This bears on V5 only as an argument. They acknowledge that polysemanticity can occur without superposition (A.4) and that superposition is hard to tell from composition (Sec 5.4), which tempers the V3 support. All models are from one family (Pythia) trained on the Pile. No row records the context-neuron monosemanticity evidence; r6 and r7 record ablation loss only.

versions.untested_parts: The share of all MLP neurons that are polysemantic is not measured; the study examines selected neurons and does not quantify prevalence across transformer layers.
The study presents evidence consistent with superposition but does not establish that capacity pressure causally produces each observed polysemantic neuron.
Polysemanticity caused by initialization, regularization, or training noise when capacity is sufficient.
Comparisons of activation functions, architectures, or regularization, and whether polysemanticity can be lowered without a large performance cost.
The paper does not test the cited InceptionV1 example or determine whether most canonical polysemantic neurons have a shared feature.
The study discusses and demonstrates sensitivity to inspection and probe choices, but does not systematically sweep activation ranges or explanation-scoring methods.

rows.subject: Pythia 70M, neuron 70M.L1.N111
rows.operation_detail: Inspected neuron activations across a broad text corpus after identifying the neuron with a compound-word probe.

conditions.value: Pile Test set; figure generated with 300 million tokens

rows.measure: Observed input patterns activating the neuron
rows.value: The neuron activated on a huge variety of apparently unrelated n-grams; the text says the displayed examples only scratch the surface.
rows.note: The authors describe this as a polysemantic neuron; the figure is illustrative rather than a quantified prevalence estimate.
rows.check: 'Observed' holds for V2 and V7. For V6 the row is counter-evidence: the authors read the n-grams as unrelated, not as one shared feature. Single-neuron case study; it gives no prevalence.

rows.subject: Pythia 70M, neuron 70M.L1.N111
rows.operation_detail: Examined the maximum-activating examples on a larger corpus.
rows.measure: Composition of the top activating examples
rows.value: 16 of the top 20 examples showed activation on the “he” of German words beginning with “Schönhe”.
rows.note: The authors use this to illustrate that conclusions depend on the corpus and examples inspected; this count does not establish that other inputs fail to activate the neuron.
rows.check: Should be observed, not partial. The top-20 view on 10B train tokens looks near-monosemantic ('Schönhe'), while the 300M-token test view shows a huge variety. Together these fully show that the verdict depends on the slice of activations examined.

rows.subject: Pythia 1B
rows.operation_detail: Trained probes to identify neurons for 21 compound words, contrasting each target bigram with examples sharing only one word.

conditions.value: 2,000 target examples and 4,000 examples for each of two negative sets per compound word
All layers probed; examples discussed in layers 1–3

rows.measure: Probe discrimination of the target compound word
rows.value: Many individual neurons were almost perfectly discriminating for the probed compound word.
rows.note: This initial probe result did not by itself reveal the other inputs that activated those neurons.
rows.check: This is the probe-dataset view, which looks near-perfectly discriminating. It bears on V7 only when contrasted with r4's wider-corpus view. On its own it is a neuron-selection result.

source_check.locator_found: Section 5.1 (almost perfectly discriminating neurons); B.2 Compound Words (2000 XY, 4000 XW, 4000 ZY)

rows.subject: Pythia 1B
rows.operation_detail: Inspected the activations of compound-word neurons over a wider text corpus.
rows.measure: Variety of inputs activating the selected neurons
rows.value: The neurons activated for many apparently unrelated n-grams and local patterns, not just the compound word used to find them.
rows.note: The text says examples for all 21 compound words are shown in the figures; it does not provide a count of polysemantic neurons.
rows.check: 'Observed' holds for V2, V3 (as evidence consistent with superposition, not proof of cause) and V7. For V6 the shared-feature reinterpretation is absent. No count of polysemantic neurons is given.

rows.subject: Pythia 1B
rows.operation_detail: Summed activations of three neurons identified for the “social security” compound word.

conditions.value: Three neurons from the same layer

rows.measure: Separation of summed activation for the target compound word from other observed token combinations
rows.value: The summed activations achieved nearly perfect separation, although the individual neurons also activated on other inputs.
rows.note: This is presented as an example of a feature represented by a combination of polysemantic neurons.
rows.check: Shows a feature carried by a sparse sum of polysemantic neurons, which is consistent with superposition. Capacity pressure is argued (A.10), not experimentally manipulated.

rows.subject: Pythia 70M
rows.operation_detail: Ablated an identified context neuron by fixing its activation to zero.
rows.value: Ablating one neuron caused an average loss increase of 8% per French sequence; other contexts were described as nearly unaffected.
rows.note: The result concerns a selected context neuron and shows context specialization, not the overall frequency of monosemantic neurons.
rows.check: Ablation loss measures the neuron's importance to the target context, not polysemanticity. The evidence that context neurons are monosemantic is in their activation distributions (Fig 3 left; Figs 15-17), which no row records.

rows.subject: Pythia 6.9B
rows.operation_detail: Ablated an identified context neuron by fixing its activation to zero.
rows.value: Ablating one neuron caused a 0.2% increase in loss per French sequence; other contexts were described as nearly unaffected.
rows.note: The paper says the impact of a context neuron depends heavily on model size.
rows.check: 'Partial' is wrong. The smaller loss increase at 6.9B reflects lower single-neuron importance at scale, not weaker specialization; other contexts remain nearly unaffected. Not a polysemanticity measure.

rows.subject: not stated
rows.operation_detail: Probed for the feature is_title using a selected neuron.
rows.note: The authors explain that this strong summary score conceals what fraction of activations actually correspond to titles.
rows.check: The model is not stated in the text (LaTeX/arXiv dataset). The row shows a high summary score that the raw counts in r9 contradict.

source_check.problem: Model is not stated in the text; row correctly says not stated.

rows.subject: not stated
rows.operation_detail: Inspected raw activation counts for the neuron probed for is_title.
rows.measure: Share of activations explained by the target feature
rows.value: The is_title feature explained less than half of the activations; the remaining activations were for section titles.
rows.note: The text does not identify the model for this example.
rows.check: Should be observed, not partial. The F1 and raw-count views give different pictures (V7). The residual activations resolve to section titles, a related offshoot (V6). The neuron was probe-selected, not a canonical polysemantic neuron, and the model is unstated.

rows.subject: Pythia 6.9B
rows.operation_detail: Identified a neuron while probing for is_passive_verb and examined its activations.
rows.measure: Probe precision and recall and interpretation of neuron activations
rows.value: The neuron had high recall and low precision; it also activated on adjacent adposition tokens and past participles in adnominal clauses.
rows.note: The paper says this pattern can indicate a neuron represents a less granular feature than the probe labels.
rows.check: The extra activations (adjacent adpositions, adnominal past participles) are a related, coarser grammatical feature, not unrelated stimuli. The authors note low precision is also consistent with polysemanticity (footnote 10).

rows.subject: Pythia 6.9B
rows.operation_detail: Identified a neuron while probing for is_verb and examined its activations.
rows.measure: Probe precision and recall and interpretation of neuron activations
rows.value: The neuron had low recall and high precision; it activated on most verbs, especially infinitives, but not on several specified verb types or dependency roles.
rows.note: The paper says this pattern can indicate that a neuron represents a more specific feature than the probe labels.
rows.check: A low-recall neuron that encodes a more specific verb feature concerns feature granularity, not polysemanticity.

source_check.notes: Same-group study: the header says it shares one author with an original, so it counts as R1, not independent. V2.support[1], V6.support[1], V7.support[0], V7.support[4] and V7.suggested_status wrongly treat it as independent. The early-layer weight statistic (first 25% of layers; Fig 2c, Fig 8) is in no row. The r8/r9 model is not stated. r1/r4 carry one state, 'observed', across V2/V6/V7; for V6 they are counter-evidence, as the verdict fix says.

statements.correction: arXiv:2305.01610 carries the shared-author mark (one author shared with an original): it is the original group's own work, not an independent test. 70M.L1.N111 (300M Pile test tokens) and the Pythia 1B compound-word neurons (21 words, layers 1-3) fire on many unrelated n-grams.
statements.problem: The 'why' says neither header carries an author-overlap mark. The pack header for 2305.01610 says SHARES AUTHORS WITH AN ORIGINAL (1 name). The r1/r4 facts are right.

statements.correction: arXiv:2305.01610 tests V3 (supports) and carries the SHARES AUTHORS WITH AN ORIGINAL mark. Its Pythia 1B evidence (r4, r5) is correlational and from the original group, not independent.
statements.problem: Calls the 2 V3 testers that share an author with an original 'unidentified in the pack' and guesses they are the Toy Models records. 2305.01610 has a V3 verdict and its header carries the shared-author mark, so it is presumably one of the 2. That makes the only real-model correlational V3 evidence same-group.

statements.correction: arXiv:2305.01610 carries the SHARES AUTHORS WITH AN ORIGINAL mark. L8.N8915 (Pythia 6.9B, is_passive_verb) has high recall and low precision, and also fires on adjacent adpositions and adnominal past participles. For the is_title neuron (model not stated), is_title explains under half of activations; the rest are section titles.
statements.problem: The 'why' says 'No SHARES AUTHORS flags'. 2305.01610's header carries that flag. The r9/r10 facts are right.

Minor: in the text the athlete reading comes from the probe (names of athletes, Fig 5a left), not explicitly from max-activating examples. The text contrasts per-token averages with max-activating examples in general.

statements.correction: arXiv:2305.01610 carries the SHARES AUTHORS WITH AN ORIGINAL mark. It probes seven Pythia models (70M-6.9B); r1-r4 use 70M and 1B. On 10B Pile train tokens, 16 of N111's top 20 examples fire on the 'he' of German words starting 'Schönhe'. Over 300M Pile test tokens it fires on a huge variety of unrelated n-grams.

(3) 'Show the target pattern': the 16 of 20 top examples fire on the 'he' of German 'Schönhe' words, which is not the probed compound word.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Selected early-layer compound-word neurons in Pythia
reader_labels.reason: Broader activation inspection found apparently unrelated n-grams and patterns for neurons located by compound-word probes (r1, r4).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The paper also reports context-specialized neurons whose ablation affects the target context much more than other contexts, with the loss effect differing by model size (r6, r7).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: Individual neurons were polysemantic, while a sparse combination of three neurons nearly separated a compound-word feature from other observed combinations (r4, r5).

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.reason: The paper reports that selected neurons activated on many apparently unrelated n-grams, rather than only a shared compound-word feature (r1, r4).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: A neuron can appear sharply tuned under a probe yet show other activation patterns under broader inspection; probe scores and raw activation counts can also give different impressions (r2, r3, r8, r9, r10, r11).
